newsitem.title: USA: Albright denies she snubbed British minister.
newsitem.headline: Albright denies she snubbed British minister.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright dismissed reports on Thursday that she was snubbing Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, and blamed scheduling problems for a decision not to see him.

"This is how misunderstandings begin," Albright said in an interview with Reuters, when asked about reports that she had called off a meeting with the minister, Sir Patrick Mayhew, in a quarrel over policy in Northern Ireland.
Albright will meet British government leaders in London next Wednesday as part of a nine-country round-the-world tour, her first overseas trip as secretary of state.

The London Times and the Irish Times quoted U.S. diplomatic sources as saying the decision to cancel the meeting was due to anger at what has been interpreted in Washington as British attempts to manipulate U.S. policy.
British media reports said that Albright was going to withdraw Jean Kennedy Smith as U.S. ambassador to Ireland and a key figure in U.S. support for the Irish peace process.
"There has been absolutely, and I underline absolutely, no attempt to do anything but arrange meetings and no intention at all of not having a meeting," Albright said.
"My staff was basically looking at ways of trying to deal with a lot of issues when I'm in London. I'll meet (him) next time," she added.
Mayhew has also denied that he was being snubbed.

Albright evaded questions over whether she was advocating a policy tougher than before on Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrilla organization fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

Washington has made no secret of its disappointment that even though it allowed Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams to make several high-profile visits to the United States, the IRA ended a 17-month cease-fire one year ago.
"I think we're concerned about violence always, and any escalation, and have made it clear that violent action is not the way to resolve this issue," Albright said.
Albright earlier this week publicly backed Britain's and Ireland's refusal to let Sinn Fein into Northern Ireland peace talks without a renewed IRA cease-fire.

"We support the decision to bar Sinn Fein from the talks until the IRA restores an unequivocal and lasting cease-fire," she told the House of Representatives International Relations Committee on Tuesday.
President Bill Clinton said on Thursday that the peace talks in Belfast, chaired by special U.S. envoy George Mitchell, still had his full support.
"I urge all those taking part, who share a commitment to democratic values, to move as rapidly as possible into substantive negotiation about the future of Northern Ireland," Clinton said.
Clinton also condemned the "callous" killing of a British soldier by a suspected IRA gunman on Wednesday night and urged pro-British loyalists in Northern Ireland to show restraint.
